newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch rate rise may be delayed 3 days - Rabobank.
newsitem.headline: Dutch rate rise may be delayed 3 days - Rabobank.

text.p: The Dutch central bank may wait three days before deciding whether to raise its special advances rate, Rabobank International said on Monday.
Rabobank said that with the guilder trading around 1.1260 to the mark, the central bank would probably not hesitate too long before bringing Dutch interest rates into line with Germany.
ABN AMRO Hoare Govett earlier said it expected a 30 basis point hike in the rate today to support the weakening guilder.
The special advances rate, which sets the tone for money market rates, is 2.70 percent, compared with 3.00 percent for its German equivalent, the repo rate.
The Dutch central bank last Thursday announced a four day special advances pact with commercial banks, which expires at 1500 GMT today, compared with seven days in the previous week.

"Today may already bring about a rate hike but it is possible that the (central bank) will announce a special advance facility for a duration of three days, just to see whether the recent guilder loss of strength tastes like a structural thing," Rabobank said in its Financial Weekly publication.

It said bringing Dutch rates into line with German ones would be logical as the Netherlands enjoyed healthy and well balanced economic growth, which did not need the exceptionally low interest rates prevailing now.
"In addition, with the guilder trading near its central parity against the mark, there is no reason not to bring key rates into line with those of the Bundesbank," Rabobank said.
The central parity rate is 1.1267 guilders to the mark.

It said that even if the special advances rate was raised to 3.00 percent and the secured loans rate was lifted to 2.50 percent from 2.00 percent, it could still be argued the Dutch enjoyed high growth, low inflation and low interest rates.
The secured loans rate is comparable to Germany's official discount rate.
But as Dutch money market rates were slightly below Germany's, the special advances rate may be raised by 10 or 20 basis points instead of 30.

"It would also be a token of confidence in the guilder which, after all, should stay structurally strong against the mark from a current account of the balance of payments perspective," Rabobank said.
The Netherlands runs a current account surplus, while Germany has a deficit.
The guilder was trading at 1.1263 guilders at 1315 GMT, compared with 1.1243 after the first rate hike on February 27.
